Same as title. Basically, why, when I bend my mechnical pencil before throwing it away, does the plastic turn white at the point of pressure? What's happening?

Example Image
Why does clear plastic become a discolored opaque white when bent?

When polymers (which plastic is made of) are strained/stretched, the polymer chains will begin to orient in the direction of the strain. Clear polymers are often amorphous, which means that the polymer chains are oriented in every direction. When you begin to stretch the polymer, the chains will slide past each other, and eventually all line up in similar directions. This is known as "strain crystallization." When the crystal size is on the order of visible light wavelength (visible light is 390-700 nm), you begin to scatter that light. This scattering appears as opaque white to our eyes. This results in a stronger strength of the polymer, in a phenomenon called "necking."

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strain_crystallization https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necking_(engineering)

There is also a possibility of "crazing," which is where microscopic cracks appear on the surface of the plastic during stress. These cracks also cause light scattering, which makes the plastic appear white.

An example of crazing at the surface of clear acrylic: http://superbitepicks.com/uploads/2/8/9/5/2895957/5927639.jpg

Counterspin: Brendan Fischer on Wisconsin Campaign Corruption, Lee Fang on Eric Holders Revolving Door (half-hour weekly media analysis show)

This week on CounterSpin, a sort of theme show on how media cover government corruption disguised as business as usual. First up: A Wisconsin court has just handed Gov. Scott Walker a “big victory,” headlines in the Washington Post and elsewhere declared. One might’ve hoped they’d lead with what the ruling–about Walker’s abuse of campaign finance rules–did for democracy and the public’s right to know who’s paying what to whom in public office. We’ll talk with Brendan Fischer, general counsel at the Center for Media and Democracy, about what just happened in Wisconsin.

Also on the show: The sense is that the joke is on anyone who’s at all surprised to see former US Attorney General Eric Holder miss nary a beat going from investigating big financial interests to representing them at law firm Covington & Burling. Elite media’s utter lack of interest in the move suggests that outrage is outre, but how might journalists talk about this sort of democracy-mocking shenanigan without normalizing it? Reporter Lee Fang writes for The Intercept and The Nation, among other outlets. He’s followed the revolving door for years; we’ll talk with him about that.
